newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - The Tariff Debate.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - The Tariff Debate.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV Political Correspondent)
Playing now at a parliament near you -- the Return of the Great Tariff debate.

It's the longest running show in federal politics -- centre stage longer than "The Mousetrap" in the West End. And, like "Jaws" just when you thought it was safe to enter the water, the protectionists rear their ugly heads again.
Two issues are hogging the limelight and neither is a particularly pretty sight.
This week John Howard had the guts to knock off the A$55 a tonne sugar tariff -- worth A$26 million to the industry and costing consumers millions in higher sugar prices.

The prime minister had to run the gauntlet of a National Party revolt, buying off party room opposition for the relatively low price of A$2 million for upgrading roads from the NSW sugar zone to export ports.

The irony is that it's New South Wales state's sugar industry with its domestic orientation which stands to struggle most to improve its efficiency in the face of the cut, but it's Queensland's National Party parliamentarians who are squealing like stuck pigs.
Perennial maverick Bob Katter's threatening to cross the floor, so too is fellow Queensland National De-Anne Kelly.

Senators Ron Boswell and Bill O'Chee are none too privately fuming. Katter will almost certainly carry his grandstanding to its inevitable conclusion. The senators will almost certainly wimp it -- because crossing the floor in the Senate would see the tariff cut legislation defeated.
The Queenslanders like to make big blokes of themselves with their own constituents, but not to the point of actually doing anything.

The same goes for the increasingly oppositionist Labor Party. After years of good work in office getting the The same goes for the increasingly oppositionist Labor Party. After years of good work in office getting the tariff down from A$115 a tonne in 1989, and pressing for further reductions, Labor's now decided it's time for a touch of opportunism.
Last week Kim Beazley made a special dash to the NSW north coast simply to "... try and box them in" -- meaning the government -- by announcing Labor would oppose any further cut in the sugar tariff.
Ah, the beauty of opposition.

As it went for sugar so it goes for cars. Just as he flew to Lismore to try and make consumers pay more for sugar so he snuck out of Canberra two Thursdays ago to Adelaide, effectively to call for motorists to pay more for their cars.

Within the next few weeks, the Howard government has to decide what to do about car tariffs beyond the turn of the century. The Productivity Commission has recommended a cut from 15 percent in 2000 to five percent in 2005.

The commission estimates tariff assistance is costing consumers no less than A$3,700 per car. (The industry's hired gun economist disputes this, putting the figure at a mere A$80.) The commission also puts the GDP boost of its recommendation for a 10 percent cut at up to A$4.5 billion.
The debate has already produced a heap of outlandish political theatre.

Wannabe reformist paragon Jeff Kennett suddenly discovered an area of economic efficiency he did not like; privatisation zealot John Olsen suddenly started talking disparagingly of economic purism; the car makers, especially Ford, threatened they'd take their bats and balls and go home; government backbenchers like Christine Gallus start to argue less than coherently against the Productivity Commission recommendation.

But most extraordinary has been the behaviour of Industry Minister John Moore. TCF is the other remaining highly protected manufacturing sector. As reported in The Australian newspaper last weekend, the minister has been actively briefing that industry on how to fend off tariff cuts.

"... an appeal to them (the cabinet dries) could be made to them based on the impact of significant industry wind-downs and loss of employment opportunities within their home electorates and home states," was the way a TCF newsletter put Mr Moore's helpful suggestions.
Whatever happened to cabinet solidarity?
Being lobbied by vested interests is one thing -- suggesting how they should fight their selfish battles is a quite amazing role for a minister.

Labor's easy hypocrisy on the subject is equally breathtaking. After years of hard work to make the car industry internationally competitive -- to the point where Australian cars are finally close to a quality and price match to equivalent imports -- the ALP has given the game away in the forlorn hope that it will regain a few regional seats.

All this, too, at a time when the signs are that the enhanced competitiveness of the industry is paying real national dividends by boosting exports. Holden engines for Daewoo cars is but the latest example.
So what do the protectionists want to do? Stop the car industry making a genuine contribution to overcoming Australia's number one economic problem -- the current account deficit.
That's what is really at stake in the tariff debate -- the country's long-term standard of living, not just easy living for a few marginal seat holders in Adelaide.
And what was it John Moore and Peter Costello were discussing at the Commonwealth Club in Canberra last Wednesday?
Is the treasurer really helping the good fight by suggesting Australia could do with one less car maker, namely Mitsubishi?
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
